name: Edinburgh Castle
label: Edinburgh Castle
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4301292: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Edinburgh Castle' (318 m across).
notes: Classic view from Princes Street Gardens.

text.description: Edinburgh Castle sits on top of Castle Rock, the remains of an extinct volcano that rose roughly 350 million years ago. That is much of why it photographs so well. The rock is about 130 metres above sea level, with cliffs to the south, west and north that drop around 80 metres to the land below. The walls seem to grow straight out of the stone, and a phone camera picks up that drama easily. The only gently sloping approach is from the east. A royal castle has stood here since the 11th century, and research in 2014 counted 26 sieges in its 1,100-year history. St Margaret's Chapel, from the early 12th century, is regarded as the oldest building in Edinburgh. Most of the other buildings are younger, because the medieval defences were largely destroyed in the Lang Siege of 1573. From the recommended spot the castle is about 251 metres away, which is far enough to fit the whole rock and the skyline into one frame. Keep the rocky slope in the lower part of the picture to show how high the castle stands, and leave some sky above the towers. Take a few shots at different zoom levels, as a closer crop shows the walls and a wider one shows the setting.
text.geographic_location: In the heart of Edinburgh, on top of Castle Rock above the city centre. The recommended spot is on the north-west side of the castle, about 251 m from it.
text.directions_text: It is about 251 m north-west of the castle, measured in a straight line from the centre of the castle outline. Follow the map and keep the rock in view ahead of you to the south-east. The phone icon on the map is about 120 m north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the whole castle and rock in one frame. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the walls and towers. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground or sky, because it makes the castle look small and far away.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 120 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. From here you see the rock and the walls together. Stay put rather than walking closer, because the cliffs would then fill the frame and cut off the top of the castle.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the castle's skyline on the upper third line, with the rocky slope filling the lower third. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. Take one shot at 1x and one zoomed in, and choose the one that suits you later.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the castle walls to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. If the day is grey, nudge the exposure up slightly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light in the early morning or late afternoon usually flatters the stonework. After dark, switch to night mode and hold the phone as steady as you can against a wall or railing.

text.access_note: The castle is cared for by Historic Environment Scotland and going inside is likely to need a ticket, so check the official site before you go; the view from outside is what this spot is about.

name: Arthur's Seat and Salisbury Crags
label: Arthur's Seat
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/31209291: the OpenStreetMap point 'Arthur's Seat'.

text.description: Arthur's Seat is an ancient extinct volcano and the main peak of the group of hills that make up most of Holyrood Park, just east of Edinburgh city centre. It rises to 250.5 m (822 ft). Beneath it, the Salisbury Crags form a line of dark basalt cliffs facing the city, which is why the view works so well. You get a rugged hillside and sheer rock close to the streets and buildings. The lava is dated at roughly 341 to 335 million years old, and a glacier later scraped away the western side to leave those crags. From some angles the whole hill is said to look like a lion lying down, and two of its old volcanic vents are called the Lion's Head and the Lion's Haunch. Robert Louis Stevenson described it as "a hill for magnitude, a mountain in virtue of its bold design". For a phone photo, treat it as a big landscape. Include some foreground, such as the city or a bit of parkland, so the hill has a sense of scale. Zooming in gives you the crags and the summit as a clean, layered shape. Keep the horizon level, and wait for a moment when the sky has some cloud in it.
text.geographic_location: Arthur's Seat sits in Holyrood Park, just east of Edinburgh city centre and about 1 mile (1.6 km) east of Edinburgh Castle. The Salisbury Crags run along the hill's edge on the city side.
text.directions_text: Head south-east and the hill will stay in view ahead of you. The phone icon on the map is about 1.1 km north-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start on the default lens (1x) for a wide view with the hill in context. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the crags and summit. Skip the ultra-wide (0.5x) here, as it will make the hill look small and distant.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 1.1 km north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the skyline of the hill on the upper third line. Fill the lower part of the frame with the city or the nearer land, so the hill looks as big as it is. Use telephoto for a tighter shot of the Salisbury Crags and the summit, and hold the phone steady with both hands, elbows tucked in.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the crags to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the rock stays dark and textured. If the haze is heavy, tapping on the hill rather than the sky usually helps.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or evening is usually best, when the low sun falls on the crags and the hill. Clear days after rain give the sharpest view.

text.access_note: Arthur's Seat and the Salisbury Crags are part of Holyrood Park; rock climbing on the crags has been banned since 2019 and the Radical Road path beneath them has been closed since 2018, so check the official site before you go for current access.

name: The Royal Mile
label: Royal Mile
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/65953: large area 'The Royal Mile' (1544 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
The Royal Mile is the main street of Edinburgh's Old Town. It is really a chain of streets: the Castle Esplanade, Castlehill, the Lawnmarket, the High Street, the Canongate and Abbey Strand. Together they run downhill from Edinburgh Castle to Holyrood Palace, and the distance is almost exactly one mile. The street falls from about 109 m above sea level at the castle to about 42 m at the palace, so it has a gentle, steady slope that shows well in a photo.

It photographs well because of the tall old tenement buildings (the 'lands') pressing in on both sides, with narrow alleyways called closes dropping away off the main street. Much of the south side of the High Street was rebuilt or refaced in a Georgian style after the Great Edinburgh Fire of 1824, and the buildings step down the hill. That gives you long, receding lines of rooftops and chimneys.

It is also the busiest tourist street in the Old Town, with shops, pubs, restaurants and visitor attractions, and the High Street gets especially crowded during the Edinburgh Fringe. So expect people in most shots. You can use them to give a sense of scale, or go early for a clearer view. Hold the phone upright for the height of the buildings, or turn it sideways to follow the street as it runs away from you. Look for a spot where the street bends or a close opens up, as these give your photo a clear focal point.
text.geographic_location: The Royal Mile runs through the Old Town of Edinburgh, along the ridge between Edinburgh Castle at the top and Holyrood Palace at the bottom. The subject sits within the Royal Mile area.
text.directions_text: From there the subject is 23 m to the west, a short walk of a few seconds. The phone icon on the map is about 25 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full height of the buildings and the sweep of the street. Use the default lens (1x) for natural-looking street scenes. Try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details such as rooflines, signs or a close entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 25 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. You are looking up the slope of the street, with the buildings on both sides leading your eye along it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the tall building edges with the vertical lines so they do not lean. Keep the street running diagonally through the frame, and include a close entrance or shopfront at the edge for depth. For a tighter shot, zoom in to 2x or more and frame a stretch of rooftops and chimneys.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest building or the sky to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing. A short Live Photo can capture the movement of the crowds.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning is likely to be quieter and gives you the street with fewer people in it. Be prepared for crowds later in the day and especially during the Edinburgh Fringe.

text.access_note: The Royal Mile is made up of public streets, but individual attractions along it may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Palace of Holyroodhouse
label: Holyrood Palace
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/16769442: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Palace of Holyroodhouse' (114 m across).

text.description: The Palace of Holyroodhouse is the King's official residence in Scotland. It stands at the bottom of the Royal Mile, at the opposite end from Edinburgh Castle, with the ruins of Holyrood Abbey beside it and Holyrood Park behind. It photographs well because the stonework, towers and open ground in front give you a clear, uncluttered view. The ruined abbey next to it adds an older, softer shape to the scene. The oldest surviving part of the palace is James V's Tower, built between 1528 and 1536. It is a big rectangular tower with rounded corners at the north-west corner, and it gives the front its castle-like look. The abbey was founded in 1128, and James IV began building a Gothic palace next to it in 1501. Mary, Queen of Scots lived in the tower's apartments in the 1560s. You get the best overall shot from a little way back, where the whole front fits in with some sky above it. Move a few steps left or right until the towers sit neatly in the frame and no lamp posts or passers-by cut across the building. Keep the phone level so the walls stay upright. Then step in or zoom to pick out details such as the tower and the windows. If you plan to go inside, check the official site before you go. Photography rules inside are not covered here.
text.geographic_location: At the bottom of the Royal Mile in Edinburgh, next to the ruins of Holyrood Abbey and on the edge of Holyrood Park.
text.directions_text: No tram stop or station is listed close to this spot, so head for the bottom of the Royal Mile, the end opposite Edinburgh Castle. Walk towards the palace and the ruined abbey beside it. The phone icon on the map is about 150 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to fit the whole palace front into the frame. Use the telephoto (2x-3x, depending on your phone) to pick out the towers and windows. The ultra-wide (0.5x) makes the palace look small and far away from here, so save it for a close-up of the gates or the ground in front, if you want a dramatic angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 150 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. From here the palace is a clear subject, with James V's Tower at the north-west corner, on the left as you face it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the base of the palace on the lower line, leaving about two thirds of the frame for building and sky. Keep the phone level so the walls do not lean. Take a wider shot first, then zoom in on the tower for a second picture. For a different view, take a close shot of the palace front through any gap in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands, and take two or three shots in case of movement.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or early evening is a good choice, as the sun should then be shining on the west front. Go early in the day if you want fewer people in the frame.

text.access_note: The palace is a working royal residence whose public apartments are open for much of the year but not when the royal family is in residence, so check the official site before you go.

name: St Giles' Cathedral
label: St Giles' Cathedral
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-14).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/42407060: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St Giles' Cathedral' (82 m across).

text.description: St Giles' Cathedral, also called the High Kirk of Edinburgh, sits in the middle of the Old Town on the Royal Mile, and it is one of the easiest places in the city to photograph. The stonework is dark and detailed, and the building is set among narrow, busy streets. That gives you a strong sense of the Old Town in one frame. The church you see today was begun in the 14th century and extended until the early 16th century. It was altered in the 19th and 20th centuries, and the Thistle Chapel was added between 1909 and 1911. John Knox was its minister after the Scottish Reformation, so the building is tied closely to Scotland's history. It is also one of Scotland's most popular visitor sites, with over a million visitors in 2018. Expect people in your shots at most times of day, so use them to show the scale of the building, or wait a moment for a gap. Look for the tower and the texture of the old stone. Tilt your phone upright to catch the height, and keep the lines straight with the gridlines on.
text.geographic_location: St Giles' Cathedral is in Edinburgh's Old Town, on the south side of the High Street, which is part of the Royal Mile. It forms the north side of Parliament Square and lies downhill from Edinburgh Castle.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the High Street section of the Royal Mile in the Old Town. From there the cathedral is 51 m to the south-west, about 1 minute on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 25 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole building as people see it from the street. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street is too tight to fit the tower and walls in. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out stonework and the top of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 25 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west. You will be looking across the street at the building, so you can fit more in than you could from right beside the walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the tower on one vertical line so the walls do not lean. Hold the phone upright to catch the height. Include a little of the Royal Mile street in the foreground to give a sense of place. Then step closer and use 2x or more for a tighter shot of the carved stone.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky does not wash out. If people keep walking through, try a Live Photo and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually quieter on the street. Soft daylight suits the dark stone better than harsh midday sun.

text.access_note: This is an active church and a popular visitor site, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and any rules on photography inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning is usually quieter on the Royal Mile than later in the day.
Soft daylight tends to suit dark stone better than harsh midday sun.
The street in front of the cathedral is narrow and often busy with people walking through.
Keeping the gridlines on helps keep tall walls looking straight in a phone photo.

name: Calton Hill
label: Calton Hill
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Princes Street Gardens' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Princes Street Gardens' (node/13444424887): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1149620440: the OpenStreetMap point 'Calton Hill'.

text.description:
Calton Hill sits at the east end of Princes Street, a rocky hill in the middle of Edinburgh and part of the city's UNESCO World Heritage Site. Its skyline is crowded with monuments, including the National Monument, the Nelson Monument and the old Royal High School, so even from a distance it is easy to pick out. Views of the hill, and from it, have long been used in photographs and paintings of the city. In 1787 the artist Robert Barker was inspired by walking here and created the world's first panorama, a 360-degree view of Edinburgh painted from the City Observatory tower.

Most advice covers the view from the top, but this spot shows the hill itself. Stand on the Mound, the slope that divides the east and west gardens of Princes Street Gardens, and look to the north-east. Calton Hill sits in the distance with the Scott Monument and the Old Town in the same wide frame. That layering of foreground, spires and hill is what makes the photo work. One photo-spot guide suggests this view could work well at sunrise.

If you want a different angle, Castle Esplanade shows the hill far off behind the city. Regent Road shows the steep southern flank rising straight above the road, with its cliff face. That last one is thinly covered, so judge it on the spot.
text.geographic_location: Calton Hill is in central Edinburgh, beyond the east end of Princes Street and between the districts of Greenside and Abbeyhill. This photo is taken from the Mound in Princes Street Gardens, looking back towards it.
text.directions_text: Head for the Mound in Princes Street Gardens, the slope between the east and west gardens, in the middle of the city. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the Scott Monument, the Old Town and the hill together. Then try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring Calton Hill closer and make its monuments easier to see.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Princes Street Gardens (the Mound, the slope dividing the east and west gardens). Calton Hill in the distance to the east, with the Scott Monument and the Old Town in the same wide frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the hill on one of the upper thirds, with the Scott Monument as a strong shape in the foreground. Keep the phone level so the skyline does not tilt. If you want a different view, Castle Esplanade shows the hill far off behind the city, and Regent Road shows its steep southern side.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the hill to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. A panorama can sweep across the whole skyline, but move slowly and keep the phone upright.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise, according to one photo-spot guide. Check the sunrise time for your date, and arrive a little early to find your spot.

text.access_note: Princes Street Gardens is a public park and Calton Hill is open hillside with monuments, but check the official site before you go for opening times and any closures or events.
claims_not_in_sources: At sunrise you would be looking roughly towards the rising sun, so the sky will be much brighter than the hill and lowering the exposure helps.
A telephoto lens (2x-5x) makes distant objects such as the hill look closer and larger in the frame.

name: Dean Village
label: Dean Village
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Hawthornbank Lane' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Hawthornbank Lane' (way/412714341): middle (35 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/248497841: the OpenStreetMap point 'Dean Village'.

text.description: Dean Village sits in a deep valley just north-west of the city centre, yet it feels a world away from the traffic above. For more than 800 years it was a grain-milling community on the Water of Leith, and at one time it had eleven working mills. Today the old mill buildings, warehouses and workers' cottages have been turned into homes, and the stone houses, river and little bridges make a very tidy scene for a phone camera. The best-known angle is from the bottom of Hawthornbank Lane, by the river. From there you can fit Well Court and the neighbouring stone houses into one frame, and on a still day the water adds reflections. The old crossing at the foot of Bell's Brae is believed to stand on the site of ancient river crossings, and the current bridge dates from the early 18th century. High above, Thomas Telford's Dean Bridge was built in 1831-2 and opened in 1833. It stands 106 feet above the water, so the village lies far below the road. Take your time on the uneven path at water level. People live here, so keep your voice down, stay off doorsteps and keep drones at home. If you have time, Bell's Brae Bridge gives a second view of Well Court's red sandstone clock tower, and Dean Bridge gives a wide look down onto the village.
text.geographic_location: Dean Village lies just north-west of Edinburgh city centre, in the valley of the Water of Leith below Dean Bridge, close to the West End and Belford Road.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed close by, so start from the West End of Edinburgh and go north-west towards the Dean Bridge area. Head down into the valley by the steep Bell's Brae to reach the river and the old bridge. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the houses, river and bridge together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the water and the frame feels tight. Use 2x or more (telephoto, depending on your phone) to pick out Well Court's details without leaning over the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Hawthornbank Lane (bottom of the lane, at the riverside (steps down to water level)). Well Court and the stone houses framed over the river, with reflections in still water. From here you look across the river to Well Court and the stone houses, with the bridges and water in view. Dean Village itself is to the north-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the river along the lower third, so the houses fill the middle of the picture and any reflection has room. Go down to the water's edge for a lower, more dramatic view, but take care on the uneven path. Shoot Well Court from outside the gate, because the courtyard is private. For a different view, try Bell's Brae Bridge for the clock tower, or Dean Bridge for a wide look down on the village.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the water or the stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky doesn't wash out. Wipe your lens first, as the valley can be damp. Try a Live Photo, which may catch a ripple, and pick the calmest moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softest. Still water gives the best reflections.

text.access_note: Well Court's courtyard is private residential property, so photograph it from outside the gate.

label: National Museum
camera_source: Commons cluster (75 photos). Moved 91 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 30 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/467226683: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Museum of Scotland' (218 m across).

text.description: The National Museum of Scotland is two connected buildings side by side on Chambers Street: the Victorian former Royal Museum and the modern Museum of Scotland. This spot is about the roof terrace and what you can photograph around it. The terrace may offer a higher, more open vantage point, with the museum's own stonework and roofline close by and the city around it. The older building was begun in 1861 and partly opened in 1866. It has a Venetian Renaissance façade and a cast-iron central hall that rises the full height of the building. The modern building opened in 1998, so the contrast between old and new is part of the picture. The Royal Museum building reopened on 29 July 2011 after a three-year restoration. The museum is free to enter and was Scotland's most visited attraction in 2025, so expect other people in your frame. On a phone, the easiest wins are wide, layered shots that include the roofline and the city beyond, plus close details of the stonework and rooftops. Keep the horizon level using the gridlines, and tap on the brightest part of the scene to stop the sky washing out. Roof terrace access and arrangements are not confirmed here, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In central Edinburgh, on Chambers Street beside the junction with George IV Bridge. The museum sits next to the University of Edinburgh's buildings.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for Chambers Street, by the George IV Bridge junction in central Edinburgh. Follow the museum's own signs and ask staff at the entrance how to reach the roof terrace. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the roofline and the sweep of the city. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a natural view, and use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out distant rooftops, spires and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (Level 7 deck of the modern museum wing; stand on the terrace and shoot back toward the building's modern structure and the sandstone blocks). The terrace deck itself, with its decking, sandstone blocks, plantings and parapet, framed against the Old Town skyline behind it. Turn around to take in the wider view from the same spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the horizon on the upper or lower third line. Use a nearby parapet, chimney or roof edge as a foreground to give depth, and keep the verticals straight so buildings don't lean. Try one wide shot and one zoomed detail from the same spot. If you want a sweep of the skyline, try panorama mode and move slowly and evenly.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sky or the brightest area, then slide the exposure down a little so the clouds keep their detail. Clean the lens with a soft cloth before you start. Turn on Live Photos or motion if you want a short moving clip of the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a dry, clear day when the terrace is open. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people.

text.access_note: The museum itself is free to enter, but roof terrace access and arrangements are not confirmed here, so check the official site before you go.

text.description:
This is the view of Edinburgh's Old Town skyline near Waverley Bridge, ranked number 9 on the map. It is a scene with plenty of detail, and a phone copes well with that.

It works best as a scene-setter: the whole skyline, with a little foreground, such as any element you can see nearby or passing people, to give a sense of place.

Start with the default lens (1x) and the gridlines switched on. Line the horizon up with a gridline so the rooftops sit level, then decide how much sky to include. If you want more of the skyline in one go, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x), but keep straight lines away from the edges of the frame, where they can lean. For a tighter shot of a single building or roofline, use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone). Tap the brightest part of the buildings to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out.

This is a working street area, so keep to the pavement and stay aware of traffic and other pedestrians while you frame your shot.
text.geographic_location: Near Waverley Bridge in central Edinburgh; the subject lies south of the stand-here point, towards the Old Town skyline.
text.directions_text: The skyline you are photographing lies to the south. The phone icon on the map is about 80 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the whole skyline. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the scene, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out individual buildings and rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 80 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level. Include any foreground element you can see for depth, and keep the tallest roofline away from the very edge of the frame. Take a wide shot first, then a closer zoomed one of any building that catches your eye.

text.description:
The Scott Monument is a tall Victorian Gothic tower, built as a memorial to the Scottish author Sir Walter Scott. It stands in Princes Street Gardens, opposite the former Jenners building on Princes Street. The tower is 61.11 metres (200 feet 6 inches) high and is made of Binny sandstone. Years of city smoke have darkened the stone, which gives it a dramatic look. That look suits photographs, and the spire is so detailed that it works as a subject by itself.

The building work finished in 1844 and the monument was inaugurated in 1846. Inside the four main columns sits a white marble statue of Scott with his dog Maida. Around the tower are 64 figures of characters from his novels that you can see from the ground. The tower also has viewing platforms, and the highest one is reached by 287 steps.

The phone icon on the map is about 80 m west of the subject. From there you can fit the whole spire in the frame with gardens and trees around it. Turn the phone upright to capture the full height. Look for the pointed pinnacles and arches rather than only the overall shape. If you want the carved figures, walk closer and zoom in, rather than trying to catch everything from one place. Some figures near the top are only clear with a telephoto lens.
text.geographic_location: The monument is in the centre of Edinburgh, in Princes Street Gardens. It is opposite the former Jenners building and close to Edinburgh Waverley Railway Station.
text.directions_text: Make your way to Princes Street in the centre of Edinburgh and look for the monument opposite the former Jenners building, close to Waverley Railway Station. The phone icon on the map is about 80 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if people or trees crowd the edges and you want more of the surroundings. Use telephoto (2x-5x) for the carved figures and the top of the spire.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 80 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Keep the whole spire in view and try to keep the sides of the tower straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the phone to portrait and switch on gridlines. Place the spire on a vertical gridline and keep the horizon level. A tree branch or a path in the foreground adds depth. For a second shot, zoom in on the upper part of the tower, where the pinnacles and the small figures are.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the dark stonework still shows detail. Phone cameras can struggle with a dark tower against a bright sky, so check the result and retake if needed.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning and the hour before sunset tend to give softer light and fewer people in the gardens. After dark, the tower has soft warm lighting, so try night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.

text.description: Greyfriars Kirkyard is the old graveyard around Greyfriars Kirk, on the southern edge of Edinburgh's Old Town beside George Heriot's School. It photographs well because so much is packed into one space: weathered headstones, carved wall monuments, tombs with domes and railings, and the church behind. Burials began in the 1560s, and the Franciscan friary that gave the place its name was dissolved in 1560. The National Covenant was signed in the kirk in 1638, and in the 1840s early photographers David Octavius Hill and Robert Adamson used the graveyard as a setting for their portraits. Many visitors come for Greyfriars Bobby, the dog said to have guarded his master's grave. Bobby's headstone stands at the entrance, put up by the Dog Aid Society in 1981, and his statue is opposite the gate at the junction of George IV Bridge and Candlemaker Row. The grave of his master, John Gray, known as "Auld Jock", lies on the eastern path about 30 m north of the entrance. For photos, look for repeating lines of headstones, the carved mural monuments along the old walls, and the Kirk as a backdrop. Keep to the paths, stay quiet near graves, and wait a moment for people to move out of your frame. The whole kirkyard is a protected category A listed site.
text.geographic_location: In Edinburgh's Old Town, at its southern edge, next to George Heriot's School. The Bobby statue is at the junction of George IV Bridge and Candlemaker Row.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from the Old Town and walk to the junction of George IV Bridge and Candlemaker Row, where the Greyfriars Bobby statue stands opposite the kirkyard gate. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole scene of headstones with the Kirk behind. Use the default lens (1x) for single monuments and the entrance. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carved details on the wall monuments, without stepping off the paths.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Candlemaker Row and George IV Bridge (southern end of George IV Bridge, on the pavement opposite the National Museum of Scotland). The small bronze Skye Terrier on its fountain, with the Kirkyard gate and Old Town buildings behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and use the paths as leading lines into the picture. Keep the horizon level, since the old stones and walls look odd if the frame is tilted. For Bobby, take one wide shot of the gate and street, then step closer with the default lens (1x) for the headstone, keeping other visitors out of the frame where you can.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out and the stone keeps its texture. In shade or dull light, tap the darkest area and hold your phone steady, or use night mode briefly for a sharper result.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, overcast light or early in the day tends to suit stone and carving, and there are usually fewer people around then.

text.access_note: The main kirkyard is a public graveyard, so check the official site before you go for current visiting arrangements; the locked Covenanters' Prison section can only be entered by arrangement with the Kirk guides or on a tour.

text.description:
The Grassmarket is a long, open square in the Old Town, set in a hollow at the south-west foot of Castle Rock. It photographs well because the ground drops away below the surrounding streets, so the castle rock and its walls rise above the rooftops, pubs and shopfronts along the north side. The view to the north has long been a favourite with painters and photographers.

It began as a market place, and from 1477 it was one of Edinburgh's main markets, with part of it used for selling horses and cattle. It was also a place of public executions. A memorial near the old gallows site, put up in 1937, remembers more than 100 Covenanters who died between 1661 and 1688. In the pavement in front of the White Hart Inn, an inscribed flagstone marks where a bomb fell during a Zeppelin raid in April 1916.

The phone icon on the map is about 110 m south-west of the subject. That gives you the whole street with the castle rock rising on one side. Take a wide shot first, then move closer for details such as shop signs, hanging baskets and the pub fronts. Stay on the pavement edges and keep clear of the road and any outdoor tables.
text.geographic_location: In the Old Town of Edinburgh, in the valley at the south-west foot of Castle Rock, just below Edinburgh Castle. The square joins West Port at its western end and Candlemaker Row and the Cowgate at its eastern end.
text.directions_text: Make your way to the Old Town and the foot of Castle Rock on its south-west side, then head for the western end of the Grassmarket near West Port. If you are coming from further away, go by taxi or hired scooter and ask for the Grassmarket. The phone icon on the map is about 110 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the whole street and the castle rock above it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the buildings feel cramped, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out castle walls, rooflines or shop signs.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 110 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. Keep to the pavement and out of the way of traffic and passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and keep the verticals of the buildings straight, with the castle rock filling the upper part of the frame. Use the pavement edge or a row of buildings as a line leading into the picture. For a second shot, use telephoto to isolate the castle walls above the roofs.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the buildings to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white. At dusk, let night mode do its work and hold the phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning is usually quietest, so you can get the street with few people in it. Late afternoon and evening bring warmer light and lit-up pub windows, but expect more people.

text.access_note: The Grassmarket is an open public street and square, but events may change what is available, so check the official city website before you go if you are planning around a particular event.

text.description:
Princes Street Gardens are two linked public parks in the middle of Edinburgh, lying in the shadow of Edinburgh Castle. This spot lies within the larger West Gardens, which cover about 29 acres (12 ha) and stretch west towards St John's and St Cuthbert's churches. The ground was once the Nor Loch, which was drained before the gardens were laid out in the 1820s. The West Gardens became a public park in 1876. That history is part of why the valley feels so open, with the Old Town rising on one side and the New Town on the other.

For a phone photo, the draw is the mix of water, lawns, flower beds and big city landmarks in one view. The fountain gives you a clear foreground, and the wide space around it lets you step back and try different framings. Other things worth a quick look while you are here are the Ross Bandstand, which dates from 1935, and the listed shelters on the upper walkway, which date from 1950.

Keep the fountain in the middle or on a third of the frame, and check that the horizon is level, since the gardens slope. Walk a few steps left or right to keep people out of the shot, or let a few of them stay in to show the scale. Look at the edges of the frame before you press the shutter, as bins and signs can creep in.
text.geographic_location: In the West Princes Street Gardens, in central Edinburgh, on the south side of Princes Street and below Edinburgh Castle. The gardens run west towards St John's and St Cuthbert's churches near Lothian Road.
text.directions_text: Head for Princes Street in the centre of Edinburgh and enter the West Princes Street Gardens on its south side. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the lawns and trees, but keep the fountain away from the edges, where it can stretch. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the fountain.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 75 m south of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. From here the fountain area sits ahead of you with open lawn and path in the foreground, so you can shoot over some clear space rather than into a crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the fountain on one of the vertical lines instead of dead centre. Keep the phone level so the fountain does not lean. Take one wide shot with the default lens (1x), then step forward a few paces and take a closer one. Portrait mode can work for a close-up of the fountain with the background softened.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the fountain to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky or water looks washed out. Live Photos can catch moving water, but hold the phone still for a couple of seconds after you press.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day usually means fewer people on the paths. Soft morning or late-afternoon light tends to flatter the water and flower beds, while midday sun can be harsh.

text.description: Circus Lane is a narrow, cobbled residential lane that bends gently between rows of mews houses, with flower displays and climbing greenery along the way. The curve leads your eye along the lane, and St Stephen's church with its clock tower stands in the background. This makes it an easy place to get a postcard-style photo on a phone. A walking guide calls the view from the North West Circus Place end the most recognisable one and the classic composition most visitors aim for. Another guide prefers the Stockbridge side as an approach, so both ends are worth a look. Stand at the end where the lane opens out and face back along the curve towards the church. Use the default lens (1x) for the main shot. Keep the clock tower in the upper third of the frame, with the cobbles and flowers filling the foreground. Early morning, around 7am to 9am, is the quietest time. The lane is narrow and people live here, so it is hard to keep others out of the frame. Cars can drive down it, so step onto the pavement when one passes, and be discreet around residents' windows and doors. Try a second shot from the junction, where the clock tower is framed over the lane.

shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on North West Circus Place (the end where the lane opens out, facing back along the curve toward the church). The curve of the cobbled lane, the mews houses and flower displays, with St Stephen's church and its clock tower in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the lane's curve on one side of the frame, with the clock tower near the upper third. For a different version, walk to the junction and photograph the clock tower framed over the lane, or try the Stockbridge end, which another guide prefers.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cobbles or the houses to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and tower keep their detail. Take a few shots in a row, and use a Live Photo if you want to choose a moment when no one is in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, around 7am to 9am, when there are fewer people.

text.description: Dynamic Earth is a science centre in Holyrood, and from outside it looks more like a pale tent than a museum. A stretched fabric roof is held up by steel masts over a steel frame, which gives the building a sweeping, sculptural outline. Behind it sits the hillside of Salisbury Crags, so the soft roof and the rough rock make a good pairing in one frame. The centre was designed by Michael Hopkins and Partners and opened in 1999, and it won a RIBA Regional Award in 2001. The site was once a gasworks and part of the old Holyrood Brewery, and the design keeps part of the original Abbey Brewery wall, so look for the surviving section of the old Abbey Brewery wall. At the front there is an amphitheatre used for outdoor events, which adds shapes and levels to a photo. The building is about 94 m across, so you will want to stand back a little to fit it all in. Keep the roof lines and masts as your main subject, and use the hill behind as a backdrop rather than trying to include everything. People walking past give a sense of scale. You do not need to go inside to photograph the exterior.

shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the main roof line on the lower third, leaving space above for sky and the hillside. text.description:
Canongate Kirk is the Church of Scotland parish church for the Canongate, in Edinburgh's Old Town. Its parish takes in the Palace of Holyroodhouse and the Scottish Parliament, and it is also the parish church of Edinburgh Castle. The building was finished in 1691, designed by James Smith, after the congregation had to leave Holyrood Abbey. The arms of Thomas Moodie, whose bequest helped pay for it, are on the facade. It is also where Zara Phillips and Mike Tindall married on 30 July 2011.

It photographs well as a calm, formal church front set among the older buildings of the street. The outline is about 47 m across, so you need a little distance to fit the whole building in. It is a short step back from the church, so you can get the whole front in one frame without craning your neck. Keep your phone upright for the height of the facade, or turn it sideways if you want to include the neighbouring buildings. Look for the coat of arms on the front and take a closer second shot of it. Be considerate of anyone going in or out, as this is a working church.

text.description: The Scotsman Steps are a stairway in Edinburgh, and they suit a phone camera well. A stairway gives you strong lines: the edges of the steps, the walls on either side and the railings all lead the eye in one direction. That makes a simple, tidy photo, and it works even if you have never thought much about composition. The walls close in around the steps, so the view feels enclosed and a little dramatic. If someone walks up or down, they add scale and a sense of life to the picture. Hold the phone upright so the stairway fills the height of the screen, and turn on the gridlines so the sides of the stairway stay straight. Tap the steps to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky at the top is bright, so the detail doesn't wash out. Take a few frames while people pass and keep the one with the best gap or the best figure. Stairways are busy places, so stay to the side and don't block the way for others. For history and background, check a local guide or the city's official visitor pages.

text.description:
The Scottish Parliament Building is the home of the Scottish Parliament at Holyrood, at the foot of Edinburgh's Canongate. It looks nothing like a traditional government building. The Spanish architect Enric Miralles designed a loose, low-lying group of buildings meant to sit in the land rather than tower over it, and that is why it photographs well. You get angled walls, big windows, leaf-shaped motifs and plenty of repeating shapes to build a picture around. Miralles spoke of the building as a gathering place coming out from Arthur's Seat, and the large windows of the debating chamber, committee rooms and Tower Buildings look out towards Holyrood Park, Arthur's Seat and Salisbury Crags.

Construction began in June 1999. MSPs held their first debate here on 7 September 2004, and the formal opening by Queen Elizabeth II followed on 9 October 2004. It won the Stirling Prize in 2005. Inside, the original lintel from Parliament House, where Scotland's old Parliament met until 1707, sits above the debating chamber.

The building is wide and low, so it is hard to fit in one frame from close up. Then walk closer and pick out details: window patterns, angled roof lines and textures in the stone and wood. Look for the crags rising behind the buildings, which show how the design relates to the landscape.
text.geographic_location: It stands at Holyrood in central Edinburgh, at the lower end of the Canongate, with Holyrood Park, Arthur's Seat and Salisbury Crags on its doorstep.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stop is listed for this spot, so start from Holyrood, at the foot of the Canongate, and head for the Scottish Parliament. The phone icon on the map is about 65 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the building. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the whole low, spreading complex in one frame, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for windows, roof shapes and surface details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 65 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. From here you can see the parliament as a whole group of buildings. Walk a little closer for detail shots.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the main run of buildings along a lower third line, leaving room for sky or the crags above. Hold the phone level, because the angled walls and roofs already add plenty of diagonals. For a second type of picture, move in close with the telephoto and frame the repeating window shapes or leaf-like motifs.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the stone and wood keep their texture. Take a few shots at 1x and 0.5x so you can choose later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light brings out the textures. A bright, even overcast day also works well, as it avoids harsh shadows across the facades.

text.access_note: The building is a working parliament, so access to the inside and to some of the surrounding areas may be restricted; check the official site before you go.
